newsitem.title: USA: Senate panel probes China link to campaign funds.
newsitem.headline: Senate panel probes China link to campaign funds.

text.p: Republican investigators on Wednesday delved into Asian American John Huang's role in an alleged plan to raise foreign funds for Democrats as the party sought to build a case that its members acted within the law.

Senate Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Fred Thompson opened the second day of hearings on campaign finance abuses, again stressing his belief that China plotted to influence the U.S. political process and its foreign policy.

But the panel's first witness, Richard Sullivan, finance director for the Democratic National Committee during the 1996 campaign, said he never saw any evidence of a Chinese effort to tamper with the elections.

"That is, I was never -- I emphasise never -- confronted at the time with any evidence or suggestion of wilful misconduct, foreign government influence, sale of office, contributions in violation of the Federal Election Campaign Act or other legal problems of that kind," he said.

Republican Sen. Arlen Specter laid out a case that Chinese arms dealer Wang Jun was a link to China's government. Wang attended a February 1996 White House reception, a visit President Bill Clinton later said he regretted had occurred.

"The public record is clear that Wang Jun has a high tie to a very high-level Chinese official and that he's the head of a major arms dealer," Specter said, telling Sullivan DNC officials should have noticed "red flags all over the place."

Republicans questioned Sullivan for more than four hours about Democratic plans to raise money from Asian Americans. They focused on efforts by White House officials and possibly the president himself to convince DNC finance chairman Marvin Rosen and party chairman Don Fowler to bring Huang on board.
Sullivan responded hesitantly at times and broke little new ground on the campaign finance abuses, which have been reported widely. He is to appear again on Thursday.

While the DNC had reservations about Huang's lack of experience in campaigns, Sullivan said in response to questions from Democrats that Huang was "most articulate" in his desire to help build support for Democrats in the Asian American community.

Huang raised $3.4 million for Democrats but about half that amount was returned as illegal or suspect. Sullivan said the party's vetting of large contributions was deficient and most of the suspect contributions were raised by Huang.

Huang would be the star witness if he testifies. The Justice Department told committee lawyers it would oppose granting him limited immunity as requested by his attorney, but the panel is free to decide immunity on its own and will continue negotiations on what he will agree to tell investigators in return for some immunity from prosecution.
Huang's lawyer, Ty Cobb, said on Tuesday his client will testify if given limited immunity. This would protect him from charges of campaign finance violations.
Huang had worked with the Indonesian Lippo Group in the early 1990s and was a senior international trade official at the Commerce Department when he sought to move to the DNC.

He was championed for the DNC post by James Riady, whose family owned Lippo, and Arkansas lawyer Joseph Giroir, who worked with Riady. The Lippo Group, a real estate and financial conglomerate, has business interests in China and donations to the Democrats by the Riadys are under scrutiny.
